title: Many Nichiren communities
hookLine: Nichiren Shu, Nichiren Shoshu, Soka Gakkai and others differ in important ways; each speaks for itself

cards: Ask a handful of Nichiren Buddhists who Nichiren was, which scroll matters most and who keeps the teaching, and the answers won't all match. Each will be sincere. Each will come with reasons, and a history of its own.
A fair listener's first job is a plain one: let each answer finish before reaching for a verdict.
That's today, and it closes a week among Japan's temple schools, from Tendai's mountain to Shingon's mandalas to the chanted title.

teach.b: Here are three, each as it describes itself, none ranked. First, Nichiren Shu. It sees itself as carrying on the temple lineages of Nichiren's disciples.
It honors Nichiren as a great teacher and bodhisattva sent to spread the Lotus Sutra, and places Shakyamuni, the eternal Buddha of the Lotus Sutra, at the center of devotion.
Its temples may hold statues as well as scrolls, and its members often chant namu myoho renge kyo. Second, Nichiren Shoshu.
It traces its line through Nikko, one of Nichiren's senior disciples, to a head temple at the foot of Mount Fuji, Taiseki-ji.

It teaches that Nichiren himself is the true Buddha for this age, and reveres one great scroll kept at the head temple as the heart of its faith. Its priests confer the gohonzon on members. Third, Soka Gakkai.
It began in Japan as a society of lay educators connected to Nichiren Shoshu. The two later parted ways, and the separation still matters to both.

Soka Gakkai now describes itself as a lay Buddhist movement, with members far beyond Japan, built on chanting, study and small discussion meetings in members' homes, and on work for peace, culture and education.
And there are others: Rissho Kosei-kai, Reiyukai, and the monks of Nipponzan Myohoji, who walk beating drums and build peace pagodas.

teach.h: OTHERS, EACH IN ITS OWN WORDS.
teach.b: Each is a sangha, and each claims to be faithful to Nichiren. They differ on who he was, which scroll is true, and whether priests or laypeople carry the teaching.
Those aren't small questions, which is exactly why each deserves to be heard in its own voice, not through a rival's summary, and not through mine.

how: Nichiren Buddhists belong to several communities, among them Nichiren Shu, Nichiren Shoshu and Soka Gakkai, which share the Lotus Sutra and the chanted title but differ on Nichiren's role, the gohonzon and the place of priests and laypeople.

games.q: a friend asks you what one of these communities believes. what do you reach for first?
o: what its rivals say about it.
games.why: today's way: start with the community's own words. each speaks for itself, and the differences are real enough to deserve that.

practice: Choose one community from today, recall one thing it says about itself in its own words, and hold that sentence for a few breaths without adding a but.
Then think of a group you belong to, a family, a team, a faith, a town, and the first sentence you'd want a stranger to hear about it. Sit with the two sentences side by side.

wordCard.voice: Many Nichiren communities. Nichiren Shu, Nichiren Shoshu, Soka Gakkai and others: one chant, one sutra, and real differences, each explained in its own voice. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Pali sangha, the community: every Nichiren group is a sangha, each with its own voice.
